title: LPIC-1 Foundations: Processes, Jobs & Priorities
purpose: Eight real-Linux lessons using the optional offline VM. Recommended sequence, no unlocks. Completion records your self-review; there is no verification score.
prerequisites: Basic command entry, paths and reading output. Use the separate GTK guest console. Start each lesson in its own session; finish its owned practice processes before leaving it.
coverage: Partial LPIC-1 v5.0 objectives 103.5 (process inspection, jobs, signals, logout persistence) and 103.6 (default/lowered priority and privilege boundaries). Not full LPIC preparation: screen/tmux/killall are absent, successful privileged priority increases are excluded, and no guest assessment is performed.

entries.description: PID, parent, owner, state and filtered process snapshots.
troubleshooting: If the process expired, start a fresh bounded sleep and immediately save its new PID.
Before signaling a saved PID, inspect owner and arguments again; PIDs can be reused.
cleanup: Use ps to confirm the actual practice PID, then kill it and wait if it is still a child of this shell.

entries.description: Terminal signals, job states, bg and fg.
troubleshooting: q is for top, not sleep; use Ctrl-C for a foreground sleep.
If bg or fg reports no such job, inspect jobs -l; the sleep may have expired or you may be in a different shell.
cleanup: Interrupt the foreground sleep with Ctrl-C. For an owned leftover background job, inspect jobs -l, terminate its actual identifier and wait.

entries.description: Accepted practice: inspect, pause, resume, terminate and reap a background job.
troubleshooting: The accepted exercise uses a five-minute sleep. If it expires, start a fresh job and update the PID/job identifier.
Use the actual job identifier from jobs -l, never assume %1 when other jobs exist.
cleanup: Verify the actual owned practice job, send TERM and wait. ps should no longer list it.

entries.description: pgrep/pkill selection, TERM versus KILL and ownership.
troubleshooting: A no-match pgrep/pkill returns nonzero; check the command arguments and whether the task expired.
Job notifications can appear at the next prompt. Inspect ps rather than relying solely on notification timing.
cleanup: Inspect the actual $first and $second PIDs before signaling. Terminate only leftover owned practice tasks and wait.

entries.description: top, watch, sorted snapshots, uptime and free.
troubleshooting: If control keys do nothing, click the guest console, not the app guidance panel.
Do not expect a deterministic top ordering or a busy VM; values vary with timing.
cleanup: Exit top with q and watch with Ctrl-C. Inspect the saved owned sleep PID, then terminate and wait.

entries.description: nohup, disown -h, controlled huponexit and logout verification.
troubleshooting: If the timer expires during reading, repeat with new bounded tasks and fresh PID records. Inspect owner and arguments before killing anything.
If exit warns about stopped jobs, resume/finish your stopped practice jobs first. Do not confuse closing GTK with logging out.
Protected processes can still end through other signals, reboot or session policy; nohup is not a supervisor or multiplexer.
cleanup: Re-inspect saved PIDs with ps. Terminate only remaining matching owned practice sleeps. Do not use broad pkill or delete evidence as a substitute for cleanup.

entries.description: Default nice value, nice, renice and denied priority increases.
troubleshooting: Use the actual PIDs and verify the programs still exist; No such process can simply mean the timer expired.
Do not assume NI equals top PR: PR is a scheduler presentation, and sleeping tasks may show no CPU difference.
Do not retry through sudo; this image intentionally has no privileged learner access.
cleanup: Inspect the three saved PIDs, terminate only those owned practice sleeps and wait for children.

entries.description: Combined practice and a guest-local handover, without new objective claims.
troubleshooting: If a task expires, document that honestly and repeat with fresh bounded tasks; do not invent observations.
Files survive a clean Stop/Resume disk; processes and shell variables do not. Re-read PID records and inspect identity, never blindly kill stale numbers.
cleanup: Re-inspect any remaining practice task. Terminate only matching owned tasks; do not treat deleting the report or stopping QEMU as normal process cleanup.
